title: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse, while Jinjiang's grassroots shoe factories ran ahead
dek: Li Honggu says Li Ning is a company made of countless mismatches: its founder had no ambition for business, held resources no one could match, and those resources became a curse instead. Jinjiang's shoe factories were started by Minnan farmers pooling household funds, carried no baggage, and made decisions purely around the market — which over the long run let them walk more steadily.
why: The industry-history section lays out rare mechanisms — household pooling, "kill the pests, protect the flowers," the mid-slope theory; the second half has Li Honggu dissecting why Li Ning was overtaken and how capital became the new curse, and that's the sharpest part.
who: Founders and investors in consumer brands, manufacturing, or family-business governance; anyone who wants to know why Li Ning and Anta took different paths.
skip: The Ding clan ancestral hall observations from 9:58 are more anecdote — fast-forward to the Nike contract-manufacturing line at 15:58.

points.h: Jinjiang is not the Fujian version of the Wenzhou model
points.body: Fei Xiaotong summed up Chinese rural development into four models: Sunan had government leading farmers to start factories, Wenzhou relied on individual entrepreneurs, the Pearl River Delta relied on foreign capital plus labor doing processing and assembly. Jinjiang appeared last and is the easiest to underestimate. It wasn't individual entrepreneurs but township enterprises started by several families and relatives pooling household funds, with a quasi-private shareholding character: in 1979, when Lin Tuqin started Jinjiang's first shoe factory, he gathered 14 village households to buy in — these people were both shareholders and employees; in 1982, when they wanted to start something new, they also split off from the original factory into five factories. The money came from Minnan's distinctive biaohui rotating credit associations, which sat in a financial gray zone, and many companies that later grew big raised their early money this way. The local government also put forward the "five permissions," allowing profit-sharing, share-based fundraising, hiring workers, and sales commissions.

points.h: Under the fake-medicine case, the government chose to kill the pests and protect the flowers
points.body: Jinjiang had two early quality crises. One was the "seven-day shoes" and "street-crossing shoes": farmers didn't understand that shoes needed specialized glue, and used ordinary glue to stick soles to uppers, so they came apart after seven days — one consumer said they came apart just from crossing the street. The second was the 1985 fake-medicine case: white sugar ground into powder, congealed into blocks, and stuffed with white fungus to pass as granules, flowing through gray channels to hospitals, reported nationwide by People's Daily. Jinjiang goods became notorious for it; over a thousand ground-promotion salesmen were turned away, and some hotels threw their luggage right out the door. At the time, Fujian's first provincial party secretary, Xiang Nan, was very market-oriented — he expanded the Xiamen special economic zone, borrowed international loans to build Xiamen airport, and called Chendai's workshops "a flower of township enterprises," but for this he was criticized as too far to the left, and after making five or six self-criticisms within half a year he stepped down. On his way out he instructed the people handling the fake-medicine case: kill the pests and protect the flowers — when you pour out the bathwater, you can't throw the baby out with it.

points.h: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse instead
points.body: Jinjiang's shoe factories were all Nike's apprentices, but the first to develop the awareness of building a domestic brand was Li Ning. Li Ning founded its brand in 1990, collecting sacred flame beneath the snow mountains of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and passing it nationwide, with enormous impact; the registration milestones of Jinjiang brands almost all come after this — Anta applied in 1990 and registered successfully in 1991, Peak was originally named Fengdeng and changed its name in 1990-1991, and 361° was previously called Bieke. But the two paths were completely different: Li Ning carried a national halo from the moment it was founded, and when performance doubled year after year in the mid-1990s it set the goal of spending ten or twenty years to put a Chinese brand in the world's number one position; the founder himself had no ambition for business and brought in professional managers, and as a result fell into crisis and internal friction again and again. Jinjiang brands were grassroots, carried no historical baggage, and made every decision around the market.

points.h: The family that gave away 51% hit every node
points.body: In 1988, Ding Shizhong was not yet 18, a middle-school dropout, and he persuaded his father to give him 10,000 yuan to buy 600 to 700 pairs of shoes, then rode two days and two nights in hard seats to Beijing, becoming one of the first Beijing drifters. Around the same time, Li Ning was running through Beijing in Li Ning-branded clothes carrying the Asian Games sacred flame. He wanted to sell Jinjiang shoes into Xidan and Wangfujing, but those were powerful state-run department stores, and a 17- or 18-year-old kid from Fujian simply couldn't get in; it took him one or two years of grinding before he got a counter. Another easily overlooked point is his father, Ding Hemu: the only male heir in the family, his family was actually weak in the village — Minnan clans fought over land and factory buildings by having many sons and by fists, and Ding Hemu didn't take part. He taught his son to give others more benefit in doing business: "give others 51% of the benefit, take only 49% yourself."

points.h: Inventory enough for the whole country to wear for three years
points.body: Around 2000, Anta signed Kong Linghui and advertised on CCTV, becoming an overnight sensation; on top of the Sydney Olympics, the men's football team reaching the World Cup, and the successful Olympic bid, the whole industry frantically signed spokespeople and opened stores, with the peak year opening close to 1,000 stores. Peak founder Xu Jingnan's metaphor was "riding an elevator": a person standing still in the elevator still rises, and everyone thought that after the Beijing Olympics they'd be on an even faster elevator. But two or three years after the Olympics the inventory crisis broke out: one manager described it as, even if Jinjiang's shoe factories stopped producing, the shoes in inventory would be enough for the whole Chinese population to wear for three years. The root cause was the distribution model of enfeoffment plus futures — ordering half a year in advance, the brand too far from the market, and distributors unwilling to share real sales data. Anta's response was to strengthen centralization, with Ding Shizhong personally touring stores like an emperor on campaign, covering 400 to 500-plus market points across China in the worst year or two.

points.h: The book is missing Nike and Adidas as the coordinate system
points.body: Li Honggu's biggest criticism of the book is that it lacks an implicit thread: Nike and Adidas's campaigns in the Chinese market actually determined the rises and falls of Chinese brands to a greater extent — they are the real coordinates. Huang Ziyi agrees, but explains that there's too little detailed material on Adidas and Nike's playbook, because multinationals have to go through procedures and discipline to accept interviews. Li Honggu also argues that Li Ning's problems can't be explained by the professional-manager system: Li Ning is "a company made of countless mismatches" — he was never happy running a business, his resource endowment far exceeded everyone else's, yet it formed a huge gap with his vision and strategy, and the resources became a curse instead. And today, after Jinjiang brands obtained capital and acquired international brands, a new problem has appeared: how to tell a story of an international brand together with your own — "capital became their curse."

points.h: Anta's multi-brand: independent front end, shared middle and back office
points.body: Anta learned FILA from someone else. Li Ning was first overtaken by Nike in 2003 and lost its market number one, and was the earliest to try multi-branding; Li Ning's first professional manager, Chen Yihong, also did very well with KAPPA. When Anta acquired FILA, at first it likewise slapped FILA labels on traditional Anta products, and only after they wouldn't sell did it learn the hard lesson and start over: in organizational structure and process, keep the FILA team absolutely independent from the Anta team, prevent them from influencing each other, then poach a world-class team to do design, move in a fashion-trend direction, and do DTC direct retail at the same time. Once that worked, Anta's multi-brand mechanism became: the retail end and the product design and R&D end are each independent, sharing Anta's powerful middle and back office, including human resources, the contract-manufacturing system, and Jinjiang's industrial cluster. What Ding Shizhong now says over and over is: I don't want to make China's Nike, what I want to make is the world's Anta.

points.h: Once per-capita GDP passes $10,000, verticals take off
points.body: When Huang Ziyi interviewed Anta in 2021, an Anta vice president explained why they acquired Amer Sports, Descente, and Kolon: based on their research in European and American markets, when a country's per-capita GDP reaches $10,000, niche sports tracks start to emerge — ice and snow, outdoor, hiking; when it reaches $20,000, these niche sports begin to flourish on a large scale. At the time of the interview China had just broken through $10,000, and now Beijing and Shanghai have already surpassed $20,000, with the national average around $15,000, so these brands taking off may be a natural process. Where Anta is stronger than others is that it may, through a relatively advanced professional-manager consciousness, have been first to do market research and lock up these tracks.

Mutual-aid lending within Minnan's acquaintance society, sitting in a financial gray zone, and the startup capital source for early factories.
The policy put forward by Chendai and Jinjiang local governments: allow profit-sharing, allow share-based fundraising, allow hiring workers, allow sales commissions.
When an enterprise reaches medium scale, if it can complete the modern-enterprise transformation it climbs further; if not, it may fall into the abyss.
The brand itself opens stores and deals directly with consumers, bypassing layer upon layer of distributors.
Weaving an entire shoe upper from a single yarn, making sneakers light and breathable, upending the leather-upper paradigm.
